summary: Defines NNTP, a protocol for distributing, querying, retrieving and posting news articles over reliable stream connections. Articles are kept in a central database so a reader can pick only the items they want, with indexing, cross-referencing and expiration of old messages. It was a proposed standard that asked for discussion and was later replaced by RFC 3977.

eli5.summary: Imagine a big library where everyone's letters to the community are stored in one room. This is the set of rules for asking the librarian for just the letters you want to read, or adding your own.

questions: how does usenet news transfer work
how do news articles get posted and retrieved
subtitle: A simple text protocol that lets news readers fetch, post and exchange articles with a central news server.

tldr.problem: Mailing lists copy every message to every subscriber, which wastes bandwidth and disk space. Hosts on a fast network would rather keep one central copy of the news and let readers pick what they want.
tldr.mechanism: NNTP is a client-server protocol with SMTP-like text commands and numeric replies over a reliable stream such as TCP, on port 119. Clients select newsgroups, read articles by number or message-id, and post new ones. Servers can also swap articles with each other.
tldr.outcome: RFC 977 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 3977, so it is no longer the current definition of NNTP.

facts.label: Text terminator
facts.value: A line with a single period

today: RFC 977 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3977, which is now the place to look for the definition of NNTP.

sections.title: Why News Needs a Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 977 starts from two ways of spreading "news" (bug fixes, product reviews, technical tips and discussions). Internet mailing lists remail a copy to every subscriber. The RFC calls this inefficient once a list grows past a dozen or so people, and it adds the work of keeping the list itself up to date.

The USENET news system stores articles once in a central repository and lets subscribers select what they want. NNTP (Network News Transfer Protocol) applies the same idea over the network: articles need only be stored on one, presumably central, host, and readers on other hosts fetch them over stream connections. The RFC argues that TCP stream connections are more general than shared file systems for serving many kinds of clients.

NNTP is modelled on the article format in RFC 850, but it makes few demands on how articles are structured, contents or stored.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing a copy of every letter to every person, keep one copy in one place and let people come and read it. That saves a lot of paper.

sections.title: The Server and Its Conversation Rules
sections.content:
The server speaks SMTP-like commands and responses over a stream connection such as TCP; the assigned contact port is 119. It is only an interface to the news database. It does no user interaction or presentation, which is left to client programs.

Commands are a command word, sometimes followed by a parameter. They are not case sensitive, end with CR-LF, and may not exceed 512 characters including the CR-LF. Text is ASCII.

Replies start with a 3-digit status code. The first digit says how the command went: 1xx informative, 2xx ok, 3xx ok so far (send the rest), 4xx correct but could not be performed, 5xx unimplemented, incorrect or a serious error. The second digit gives the category, such as newsgroup selection, article selection, distribution or posting.

When a reply is followed by text, the text ends with a line holding a single period. A text line that begins with a period has that period doubled so it cannot be mistaken for the end marker.
sections.eli5: You send short typed requests and the server answers with a number that tells you if it worked. Long answers end with a lone dot, like the period at the end of a sentence.

sections.title: Reading Articles
sections.content:
A client first picks a group. LIST returns the valid newsgroups, each as a line of group last first p, where p is y or n for whether posting is allowed. GROUP selects one and replies 211 with an estimated article count and the first and last article numbers.

The server keeps a current article pointer. GROUP sets it to the first article, and NEXT and LAST move it. ARTICLE, HEAD, BODY and STAT retrieve an article, only its header, only its body, or just its status. Each can name an article by number in the current group, or by message-id in angle brackets. Using a message-id does not change the current article pointer.

Message-ids come from the article's Message-ID header, as required by RFC 850. If the header is missing, the server supplies 0 inside the angle brackets. Because message-ids are unique, a reader can use them to skip duplicates posted to several groups.
sections.eli5: The server remembers which letter you are looking at. You can step forward or back, or ask for a letter by its unique name.

sections.title: Posting and Exchanging Articles
sections.content:
To submit a new article, a client sends POST. The server answers 340 to ask for the article or 440 if posting is not allowed. The client sends the article in RFC 850 format, ends it with a line holding a single period, and receives 240 on success or 441 on failure. The greeting on connection (200 or 201) already tells the client whether posting is allowed. The server does not filter or reformat the text.

NNTP also lets hosts feed each other without the waste of flooding every article everywhere. A host asks NEWGROUPS for groups created since a given date and time, and NEWNEWS for the message-ids of new articles. Group patterns may use an asterisk wildcard and an exclamation point to include or exclude groups. The client fetches only the ones it wants and lacks. It can then offer its own new articles with IHAVE, and the server answers 335 to receive the article or 435 if it already has it.

Other commands are HELP, QUIT and SLAVE, which marks a connection as coming from a subsidiary server. Extra commands should begin with the letter X.
sections.eli5: Servers can ask each other, "What is new since yesterday?" and then only copy the letters they do not already have, instead of everyone sending everything to everyone.

sections.title: Sample Sessions and Reply Codes
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC walks through six hypothetical sessions: reading with NEXT, reading by article number, listing new groups, posting, a server shutting down on operator request (reply 400), and a host-to-host exchange using NEWGROUPS, NEWNEWS, ARTICLE and IHAVE. It also lists every command and reply code in one place, and ends with a short note on how USENET stores articles as one file each in a spool area.

The codes in the second digit also reserve room for private extensions (x8x) and debugging output (x9x). Unspecified codes must not be used for standard commands.
sections.eli5: The document ends with pretend chats between a reader and the server, so you can see what a real conversation looks like.
